summary: Sustained throughput degradation in dedicated pool due to long-lived keepalive connections holding GPU credits
description:
Issue summary: ParcelFlow is observing a sustained p50/p95 throughput drop in their dedicated GPU pool beginning ~2026-03-10 08:30 UTC. Traffic rate to the route is unchanged; however overall batch attach success rate and effective GPU credits available for the pool have gradually declined leading to queuing and p50 increase. Impact: customer-facing QPS reduced ~35% at 10:00 UTC and p95 latency increased by ~2.5x. This is customer-visible for their streaming and short inference routes. Environment: Dedicated pool (reserved cluster) in us-west-2 backing ParcelFlow's tenant; models listed above. Steps to reproduce: 1) Import ParcelFlow test harness with long-lived keepalives (SDK v1.8.2) 2) Ramp to pre-failure normal QPS 3) Observe connection count per tenant and per-allocator socket, then watch allocator/gpu-credit metrics over 1–3 hours. Observed logs & metrics:
- slow but persistent growth in "allocated_socket_count" for the tenant (graphs linked)
- GPU-credit balance metric declines ~0.6 credits/min until autoscaler cannot attach new slots fast enough
- many long-lived connections reported in telemetry (timeouts not present; connections remain ESTABLISHED)
- allocator logs show frequent 'slot reserved but not used' events and repeated small attach attempts (see Sentry link). Initial hypothesis: a change in the customer's SDK usage pattern (long keepalive + infrequent request bursts) is consuming socket slots and preventing the allocator from reclaiming GPU credits, causing autoscaler to see low free capacity and delay scale actions. Consequence is noisy-neighbor-like starvation for short-burst routes and degraded batch packing efficiency.
comments: 2026-03-10 09:05 - Support (Leah Chen): Opened ticket with customer-provided telemetry and Grafana links. Requested a short-term mitigation: reduce keepalive TTL or enable connection pooling on client side.

2026-03-10 09:42 - ParcelFlow (Sara Holt): Confirmed they rolled back a new SDK configuration deployed yesterday that increased connection reuse. Rolled back at 09:30; seeing marginal improvement but throughput still not recovered to baseline.

2026-03-10 11:00 - SRE (Ravi Patel): Investigating allocator and autoscaler logs. Noted repeated reservation events where a socket remains reserved for >5m without issuing an inference. Added probe to log attach/release sequence for the tenant.

2026-03-11 02:20 - Engineering (Marcus Rivera): Observed allocator token-bucket depletion pattern when many connections hold reservations concurrently. Proposed quick fix to allow aggressive reclamation for sockets idle >60s in dedicated pools if tenant is in dedicated tier.

2026-03-11 14:07 - Support (Leah Chen): Customer applied client-side mitigation (keepalive reduction from 15m to 45s) per our guidance. Noted immediate drop in long-lived connection count and gradual recovery of GPU-credit metric. Customer still sees residual p95 latency spikes during afternoon bursts; tracking.

2026-03-12 08:15 - Engineering (Ravi Patel): Deployed hotfix (PR linked) to allocator: reclaim idle reservations after 60s for dedicated pools and emit metric allocator.reclaims.force. Monitoring for regressions; no negative signals in e2e smoke tests.
2026-03-12 11:38 - ParcelFlow (Sara Holt): Post-hotfix: baseline throughput restored to ~95% of pre-incident. Noted one small spike during a scheduled batch job; asked about longer-term safeguards.
2026-03-12 12:05 - SRE (Ravi Patel): Marking as In Progress; recommended follow-up actions: runbook update, autoscaler tuning for mixed keepalive patterns, and SDK guidance to customers.
investigation_notes: Telemetry review showed a slow, linear draining of gpu-credit for the dedicated pool over ~4 hours prior to alerting. Drain correlated tightly with rising count of ESTABLISHED sockets from ParcelFlow's tenant.

Allocator logs: identified ~8k 'reservation_held' events in the window where reservation duration > 120s. Many reservations were never consumed for >30s following creation (pattern consistent with long-lived keepalives waiting for next request).

Autoscaler behavior: autoscaler waits for free credit threshold to fall below X before scaling. With steady reservation hold, perceived available capacity stayed low and scaling decisions were suppressed, delaying attach of new GPUs.
resolution: Workaround applied and platform hotfix deployed. Short-term: customer reduced client keepalive TTL (from 15m to 45s) and enabled connection pooling which immediately dropped idle reservation counts. Platform: hotfix merged (allocator PR) to forcibly reclaim idle reservations in dedicated pools after 60s and emit allocator.reclaims.force metric. Autoscaler has a follow-up tweak scheduled to be conservative when reclaim metrics spike. Customer confirmed throughput restored to ~95% of baseline; continued monitoring for 72 hours. Follow-ups: update keepalive guidance in SDK docs, add runbook entry for noisy keepalive symptoms, and schedule an autoscaler policy review (ENG-OPS sprint).
root_cause: Combination of a customer-side change in SDK connection behavior (long-lived keepalives with bursty usage) and conservative allocator/autoscaler heuristics that allowed reservations to be held without reclamation. This produced a capacity illusion (low free credits) and delayed autoscaler actions, causing degraded effective throughput in the dedicated pool.
next_steps: Document: Add a short troubleshooting section to the dedicated-pool runbook describing keepalive-induced GPU-credit drain and the immediate remediation steps.
SDK: Add guidance and a recommended default keepalive TTL for dedicated customers in the SDK README and changelog.
Autoscaler: Evaluate policy change to factor allocator.reclaims.force into scale decisions; run a canary for 2 weeks.
Customer: Follow up with ParcelFlow in 72 hours for final closure and offer postmortem summary.
Monitoring: Create an alert on allocator.reclaims.force > 50/min for a dedicated pool to flag noisy-keepalive patterns early.
